title: Factors, Multiples and Primes: Prime Factorisation, HCF and LCM
seo_title: Sec 1 Factors, multiples and primes Worksheets: Free Secondary 1 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: primes and prime factorisation; finding highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM), squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots by prime factorisation
meta_desc: Free Secondary 1 maths worksheets on factors, multiples and primes: prime factorisation in index form, highest common factor, lowest common multiple and HCF/LCM word problems. 100 questions with worked answers.
key_big: Every number above 1 is a product of primes: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5.
key_sub: HCF: the biggest number that divides both. LCM: the smallest number both divide into.
body_html:
How it works

A factor divides a number exactly. A multiple is in its times table. A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself (1 is not prime).

Every whole number above 1 can be written as a product of primes. Use a factor tree and keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime.

Example

Write 60 as a product of prime factors.

60 = 6 × 10 = 2 × 3 × 2 × 5.

Put in order with powers: 2² × 3 × 5.

Answer: 2² × 3 × 5

Example

Find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18.

Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. HCF = 6.

Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. 36 is also a multiple of 18, so LCM = 36.

Answer: HCF 6, LCM 36

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up factors (they go into the number) and multiples (the number goes into them).
  • Thinking 1, 9 or 51 is prime. 1 has one factor; 9 = 3 × 3; 51 = 3 × 17.
  • Stopping a factor tree at a number that is not prime, such as 4 or 9.
  • Giving the product as the LCM: 12 × 18 = 216 is a common multiple, but the lowest is 36.

faq.a: No. A prime number has exactly two factors. 1 has only one factor, itself.

faq.q: How do I find the HCF using prime factors?
faq.a: Write both numbers as products of primes. Multiply the primes they share, using the lower power of each.

faq.q: How do I find the LCM using prime factors?
faq.a: Multiply every prime that appears in either number, using the higher power of each.

faq.q: When do I use HCF or LCM in a word problem?
faq.a: Use HCF when you split things into the largest equal groups. Use LCM when things repeat and you want when they next happen together.

items.q: Bus A leaves the station every 12 minutes and bus B every 18 minutes. Both leave at 8:00 am. After how many minutes do they next leave together?
items.e: This is the LCM of 12 and 18: 36 minutes.

items.q: There are 24 pencils and 36 rubbers. They are shared into identical bags with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of bags that can be made?
items.e: This is the HCF of 24 and 36: 12. Each of the 12 bags has 2 pencils and 3 rubbers.

items.q: A floor is 12 m by 18 m. It is covered with the largest possible square tiles, with no cutting. What is the side length of each tile?
